overview:
Adipurana (Ādi Purāṇa) is a seminal Digambara Jain epic in Sanskrit, traditionally attributed to Acharya Jinasena and completed in the 9th century CE under Rashtrakuta patronage. It narrates the life and previous births of Ṛṣabhanātha (Rishabha, Adinātha), the first Tirthankara, situating his story within vast Jain cosmological cycles. The text belongs to the Prathamanuyoga (narrative literature) and is composed in mahākāvya style, blending ornate poetry with doctrinal exposition. Together with Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa, it forms the Mahāpurāṇa, a cornerstone of Digambara narrative tradition.

The Adipurana presents Ṛṣabha as a culture hero and lawgiver who inaugurates human civilization. It describes the origin of arts, writing, numeration, and various livelihoods through the teachings given to his children—especially his daughters Brahmī and Sundarī and his sons Bharata and Bahubali. The text explains the emergence of social order and kingship, including a varṇa-like classification based on qualities and actions rather than birth, reflecting Jain ethical and philosophical perspectives on society. In this way, Adipurana functions simultaneously as sacred biography, cosmological narrative, social treatise, and ethical guide.

Structurally, the work is organized into numerous parvas (cantos) that trace the soul’s journey toward perfection. Early sections focus on cosmology and the pre-birth history of Ṛṣabha’s soul, followed by his birth, royal life, and the establishment of civilization. Subsequent portions narrate his renunciation, ascetic practices, attainment of kevala-jñāna (omniscience), and teaching activity. A major narrative arc centers on the conflict between his sons Bharata, the universal monarch (cakravartin), and Bahubali, whose duel and subsequent renunciation exemplify the conquest of inner passions over external power.

The epic culminates in the liberation (mokṣa) of Ṛṣabha and the resolution of the Bharata–Bahubali conflict through Bahubali’s profound detachment and spiritual realization. Throughout, Adipurana integrates core Jain doctrines such as ahiṃsā (nonviolence), aparigraha (non-possession), self-restraint, and the workings of karma, using narrative episodes to illustrate how worldly ambition, attachment, and violence obstruct liberation. Its portrayal of Bahubali’s ascetic victory became foundational for later Jain devotion and iconography, especially the famous Gommateśvara statue at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa.

Beyond its religious significance, Adipurana has had a lasting impact on South Asian literary and cultural history. It influenced numerous medieval Jain purāṇas and inspired regional adaptations, most notably the 10th-century Kannada Adipurana by Ādikavi Pampa, which helped inaugurate the classical age of Kannada literature. The Sanskrit Adipurana and its adaptations continue to be studied as key sources for Jain theology, ethics, cosmology, and the historical development of Jain narrative art.

primary_sources.title: Ādi Purāṇa (Adipurana)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Jinasena (Digambara monk)
primary_sources.original_text: जन्मना सर्वे नराः समाना भवन्ति, भेदस्तु तेषां मार्गेण यत्र यत्र आध्यात्मिके प्रगत्यन्ति।
primary_sources.transliteration: janmanā sarve narāḥ samānā bhavanti, bhedas tu teṣāṃ mārgeṇa yatra yatra ādhyātmike pragatyanti.
primary_sources.translation: By birth all men are equal to one another; they differ only in respect of the progress they make on the spiritual path.
primary_sources.notes: This oft-cited verse encapsulates a key ethical insight of Adipurana: spiritual status is determined by inner progress, not birth. The text, composed in 9th-century Sanskrit under Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarṣa I, narrates the life of Ṛṣabhanātha, his previous births, the establishment of social order, and the paradigmatic careers of Bharata and Bahubali. It is regarded as one of the finest works of the Prathamanuyoga and forms the first part of the Mahāpurāṇa, completed by Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa.

primary_sources.title: Mahāpurāṇa (Ādi Purāṇa and Uttarapurāṇa)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Jinasena (Ādi Purāṇa) and Acharya Guṇabhadra (Uttarapurāṇa)
primary_sources.original_text: ऋषभदेवस्य चरितं आदौ विस्तरेण निरूपितम्, ततः शालाकपुरुषाणां कथाः उत्तरपुराणे प्रपञ्च्यन्ते।
primary_sources.transliteration: ṛṣabhadevasya caritaṃ ādau vistareṇa nirūpitam, tataḥ śālākapuruṣāṇāṃ kathāḥ uttarapurāṇe prapañcyante.
primary_sources.translation: The life of Ṛṣabhadeva is expounded in detail at the beginning, and thereafter the stories of the great personages (Śalākapuruṣas) are elaborated in the Uttarapurāṇa.
primary_sources.notes: Mahāpurāṇa is the composite designation for Jinasena’s Ādi Purāṇa and Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa in Digambara tradition. While Ādi Purāṇa focuses on Ṛṣabha and his immediate lineage, Uttarapurāṇa extends the narrative to other exemplary figures. Together they provide a comprehensive purāṇic framework for Jain cosmology, ethics, and sacred biography, and are central to Digambara narrative canon.

primary_sources.title: Kannada Adipurana (Ādipurāṇa in Champu style)
primary_sources.author: Ādikavi Pampa
primary_sources.translation: Adipurana, composed by the poet Pampa, is a compendium of the ten lives of Adinatha.
primary_sources.notes: Pampa’s 10th-century Kannada Adipurana adapts Jinasena’s Sanskrit narrative into champu style (mixed prose and verse) and is considered the first major work of classical Kannada literature. It focuses on the ten lives of Adinātha and popularizes key episodes—such as the Bharata–Bahubali conflict—for a regional audience. While not a primary Sanskrit source, it is an important early vernacular retelling that reflects Digambara Jain tradition and extends the influence of Adipurana into Kannada literary culture.

misconceptions.myth: Adipurana is simply a sectarian biography of Ṛṣabhanātha with limited doctrinal content.
misconceptions.reality: While Adipurana does center on the life of Ṛṣabhanātha, it is also a comprehensive doctrinal and cultural epic. It integrates Jain cosmology, ethics, social theory, and the origins of arts and livelihoods, functioning as a mahākāvya, purāṇa, dharma text, and cultural history within the Digambara tradition.

misconceptions.myth: Adipurana teaches a rigid birth-based caste system similar to some Hindu Purāṇas.
misconceptions.reality: Adipurana describes social ordering and varṇa-like categories, but emphasizes qualities, actions, and ethical conduct rather than birth as the basis of distinction. Its famous verse on equality by birth and differentiation through spiritual progress underscores a Jain perspective that prioritizes inner development over inherited status.

misconceptions.myth: The Kannada Adipurana by Pampa is an entirely independent work unrelated to Jinasena’s Sanskrit Adipurana.
misconceptions.reality: Pampa’s Kannada Adipurana is explicitly based on Jinasena’s Sanskrit Adipurana and adapts its narratives into champu style for a regional audience. It preserves core Digambara Jain themes and episodes—especially concerning Adinātha, Bharata, and Bahubali—while contributing to the growth of Kannada literature.

misconceptions.myth: Adipurana and Uttarapurāṇa are two completely separate texts with no structural or theological connection.
misconceptions.reality: In Digambara tradition, Ādi Purāṇa and Uttarapurāṇa are closely linked and collectively known as Mahāpurāṇa. Ādi Purāṇa focuses on Ṛṣabhanātha and his lineage, while Uttarapurāṇa extends the narrative to other Śalākapuruṣas. Together they form a unified purāṇic corpus that shapes Jain narrative theology and cosmology.
